metaDescription: Six corded electric snow blowers compared, 20 to 23 inches wide, with auger material, depth and cord advice for short paved driveways.
expertTake: The Westinghouse WSnow22 is the best all-round corded machine thanks to its steel auger and 22-inch path, while the WEN 5670 is the value pick with a long throw. The DEKOPRO 23-inch is the widest option for a wide drive. If your driveway is more than about 60 feet from an outlet, buy a battery machine instead. A heavy outdoor cord is part of the purchase.
introParagraphs: A plug-in machine is the simplest way to deal with a short paved drive. There is no fuel to store, no pack to keep warm and no engine to tune, so the motor runs for as long as the outlet has power and the cord reaches.

That simplicity comes with limits that shape every purchase. Reach is set by the cord, depth by a single auger that scrapes the pavement, and durability by what the auger and housing are made from. Those three things matter more than the motor rating, because almost every machine here uses the same fifteen-amp class motor. A good cord is part of the purchase, not an afterthought.

products.name: Westinghouse WSnow22 22-inch corded blower, steel auger
products.description:
The WSnow22 pairs a 22-inch path with a rubber-tipped steel auger and a stated capacity of 840 pounds per minute. The steel auger is the key detail, because plastic augers on cheaper corded machines chip on ice ridges and frozen slush, while steel flights with rubber tips tolerate both.

Against the WEN 5670 it is 2 inches wider and throws about 4 feet shorter, since WEN quotes 29 feet against 25. Against the PJH 20-inch it gives up a little motor speed but gains width and a more established listing. Dual LED lights and 7-inch snow-grabbing wheels help in the dark.

Ownership is minimal. Use a heavy outdoor cord, inspect the rubber tips each season and clear any jam with the plug pulled. It is a single-stage, so it will not cut a plow berm. If you only buy one corded machine and want the least regret, this is the model to pick.
products.bestFor: Most short to medium paved drives near an outlet. Pick it for the combination of steel and width.
pros: Steel auger resists frozen slush and ridges
22-inch path with 840 lb per minute rating
Dual LED lights for dark mornings
No fuel or battery to maintain
cons: Cord limits reach and needs care
Single-stage design will not cut heavy berms

products.name: WEN 5670 20-inch corded electric snow thrower, 15A
products.description:
The 5670 is a 15 amp, 20-inch machine that WEN rates for up to 900 pounds per minute and a 29-foot throw. Its 10-inch clearing depth is a bit deeper than the 6-inch figure quoted on some rivals.

That long throw is the standout. Where a 25-foot machine drops snow at the edge of a lawn, a 29-footer clears the berm, which matters on a narrow lot. Against the WSnow22 you lose 2 inches of path but gain throw and a higher stated capacity.

Dual LED lights are standard. The usual cord rules apply, and the machine is best on short to medium paved drives with an outlet close by. Buyers on a narrow lot with a hedge or fence beside the drive will appreciate the extra distance more than the extra inches of width.
products.bestFor: Narrow lots where throwing snow far matters. Pick it when throw matters most.
pros: Up to 900 lb per minute rated
cons: Narrower path than the 22 and 23-inch models

products.name: DEKOPRO 23-inch corded electric snow blower, 15A
products.description:
The DEKOPRO is the widest machine here at 23 inches, with a 12-inch clearing depth and a motor spinning up to 3,300 RPM. The headline figure is the path: against a 20-inch machine it removes roughly one pass in seven on a standard drive.

A wider body is a double-edged tool. It saves passes on a wide drive but is harder to turn between a car and a wall, and it needs more garage space. It also spreads the same 15 amp motor over a larger path, so dense snow is better handled by the narrower WEN or the PJH.

Expect the standard corded routine: heavy cord, plug pulled before clearing a jam, and a wipe-down after use. Check the auger material on the listing you buy, since plastic augers wear faster. If your garage door is narrow, measure the housing before ordering.
products.bestFor: Wide drives with light to moderate snow. Pick it when you want fewer passes.
cons: Wider body is harder to store and turn
Motor works harder in dense snow

products.name: PJH 20-inch corded snow blower, steel auger, 1,800W
products.description:
The PJH combines a steel auger with smart overload protection, which senses a jam from a rock or ice and cuts the motor before it burns out. That is a feature few corded rivals advertise, and it is useful because jams are the commonest way to kill a small electric motor.

The 20-inch path and 3,000 RPM motor match the entry class. Against the WSnow22 it gives up 2 inches of width but offers a protection feature the Westinghouse does not list.

Use the same cord discipline as any corded model, and still unplug the machine before clearing a jam by hand. The feature will not save a bent auger shaft, but it can prevent a burned winding.
products.bestFor: Drives with frozen slush or occasional debris that cause jams. Pick it when jams are the concern.
pros: Smart overload protection guards the motor

products.name: Snow Joe SJ627E 22-inch corded snow blower, 15A
products.description:
The SJ627E is the familiar 22-inch corded Snow Joe, with a 15 amp motor, a 13-inch intake depth and a plastic auger. Its dual LEDs and 180-degree chute follow the pattern of the category.

Its 13-inch depth is the deepest in this group, but the plastic auger limits how rough a surface it should meet. Against the WSnow22 it offers the same width and capacity with a plastic rather than steel auger.

Choose it if brand familiarity and widely available parts matter. Otherwise, a steel-auger model lasts longer on a rough drive. If you are comparing it with the WSnow22, the real differences are the auger material and intake depth.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a familiar brand and a deep 13-inch intake. Pick it when the brand name matters.
cons: Plastic auger wears on rough surfaces

products.name: PowerSmart 21-inch corded blower, 15A, 1,020 lb/min
products.description:
The PowerSmart quotes the highest capacity in the group at up to 1,020 pounds per minute and a 30-foot throw, with a 21-inch path. Its listed clearing depth is only 6 inches, which is the limiting figure.

That shallow depth means it is best for fresh snow of a few inches. A big capacity number does not help if the housing cannot take a tall pile. Against the WEN 5670 it throws about a foot farther but clears 4 inches less depth.

Push-button start and a light frame make it easy to use. Check the cord and keep the plug dry. It suits owners who clear often, early and lightly rather than after a big storm.
products.bestFor: Frequent light snowfalls where a long throw matters. Pick it for frequent light dustings.
pros: Up to 1,020 lb per minute rated

buyingCriteria.explanation: Steel augers, as on the Westinghouse WSnow22 and PJH, tolerate frozen slush and edge ridges. Plastic ones, as on the Snow Joe SJ627E, are lighter but chip. If your drive has rough edges or you often meet ice, the steel option is cheaper over several winters. Plastic flights are cheap to replace but you will notice them rounding off after a season on rough pavement, and a rounded flight leaves a thin film of snow behind every pass. Inspect the auger tips and flights before each season and replace them as a set.

Corded models run from 20 inches on the WEN and PJH to 23 on the DEKOPRO. Width saves passes on a wide drive but makes the machine bulkier. Measure your garage and side gate before choosing the widest. A useful check is to count your usual passes: a 20-foot-wide drive takes roughly nine passes at 23 inches but ten at 20, so the saving is smaller than the spec suggests once you allow for overlap. Wider machines are also heavier to lift into a car trunk or onto a shelf.

Depth ranges from 6 inches on the PowerSmart to 10 on the WEN, 12 on the DEKOPRO and 13 on the SJ627E. The deepest-intake machines can take taller piles without a second lift. A 6-inch intake means the machine pushes taller snow rather than ingesting it, which is why heavy snow tends to stall shallow-intake machines.

The PowerSmart quotes 30 feet, the WEN 29 and several others 25. Throw matters where the bank is far from the drive edge or when wind pushes snow back. Wind and wet snow shorten these figures, so treat them as best-case ranges. A chute that turns easily with a glove on is worth as much as an extra few feet of range.

All draw 15 amps at 120 volts. Use a heavy-gauge outdoor cord as short as practical, plug into a ground-fault outlet and avoid sharing the circuit with a heater. Never use a cord with exposed copper or a missing ground pin, and keep connectors off wet snow with a cord clip or a loop through the handle.

Every corded machine here is single-stage. Snow past about 8 to 10 inches, thick crust, plow berms or gravel exceed what it can do. Choose a two-stage or a shovel for those. A shovel is the right tool for the ridge a plow leaves at the end of the drive, and the machine is best after that is broken.

howWeEvaluated.title: Auger build
howWeEvaluated.description: We split the lineup into steel and plastic augers. Steel is the better long-term choice on rough drives. We noted the PJH adds overload protection. This matters most for owners with rough pavement.

howWeEvaluated.title: Width and depth
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared widths from 20 to 23 inches and depths from 6 to 13 inches. A wide machine with a shallow intake is a poor match for settled snow. A shallow intake limits a wide path.

howWeEvaluated.title: Throw and capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared throws of 25 to 30 feet and capacities of 840 to 1,020 pounds per minute. We treated these as relative figures. None of these figures are guarantees.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership burden
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed cord handling, auger wear and storage. Corded machines have no engine or battery. Cord quality is the hidden cost of corded ownership. A trip risk also counts.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to driveway
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each model to a drive width and snow depth. This is an editorial assessment, not a measured score. Buy for your worst storm, not your average one.

howToChoose.intro: Corded machines are sized by drive width and by how far the outlet is from the work area, so start with those two measurements.

rows: Steel auger with the widest standard path

howToChoose.note: Prices move, so compare current listing prices with auger material and width before choosing.
howToChoose.intro: Corded models cost far less than battery machines to run, so the budget question is mostly about auger material and width.

cards.label: Steel
cards.text: The WSnow22 and PJH use steel flights. They resist ice and rough pavement but weigh a little more. Rubber tips on both are replaceable and cheap.

cards.label: Plastic
cards.text: The SJ627E uses plastic. It is light and quiet but chips on ice ridges and frozen slush. A chipped flight can be swapped but it is easier to start with steel.

howToChoose.note: Choose steel on a rough or icy drive; plastic is fine on smooth pavement with fresh snow.

howToChoose.intro: Throw distance and intake depth pull in different directions on a small motor, so decide which matters more for your lot.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A 20-inch path and a light body so the machine stores easily. A short drive does not need the widest model.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The WEN 5670 and PJH 20-inch fit small drives, while the DEKOPRO is overkill. A smaller machine also stores more easily beside a car.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your drive is rough or icy. The steel-auger WSnow22 will outlast a plastic one. Buying a second heavy extension cord is a better use of money than upgrading to a bigger motor.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your drive is smooth and snow is light. The PowerSmart or WEN do the job. Light snow and smooth pavement are the conditions where these machines are most forgiving.

maintenance.why: A damaged cord is a shock and fire risk. Check the section nearest the plug where it flexes most. Replace any cord with exposed copper immediately.
Rubber tips wear and lose bite. Replace them in pairs to keep the auger balanced. Keep spare tips with the machine.
Slush freezes overnight. A dry rag takes less than a minute.

maintenance.task: Clear jams with the plug pulled
maintenance.why: A stalled auger can restart. Wait for the auger to stop turning first.
A dry shelf protects the motor. Coil the cord loosely to avoid kinks. Check the housing for rust spots when you put it away.

faq.q: How long a cord can I use?
faq.a: Keep it as short as practical and use heavy gauge. A long thin cord drops voltage and heats the motor. A good rule is to stay under 50 feet where possible. A ground-fault outlet is the safest choice outside.
Steel is better on rough or icy surfaces. Plastic is fine on smooth drives. If you are unsure, steel is the safer choice.

faq.q: Can a corded blower handle wet snow?
faq.a: It handles a few inches slowly. Take thin layers and let the auger clear. Waiting for the sun to soften slush also helps. A second pass is better than forcing a thick first one.
It cuts power when the auger jams so the motor does not burn out. It is a useful but not essential feature. It does not make the motor immune to a long thin cord.
It never runs out, but it is limited by cord reach. Cordless moves freely. Many owners keep a corded unit for the drive and a shovel for steps. Many owners keep both for different jobs.

faq.q: Will it clear a plow berm?
faq.a: No. Break the ridge by hand first. Use a hand shovel on the ridge, then the machine on the rest. That keeps the housing from packing with solid ice.
